vignette:
Mr. Tran sits across from me, his hands resting on his knees. They are the hands of a man who has spent a lifetime working with nets and lines-calloused, scarred, with knuckles like worn river stones. For sixty years, those hands knew their purpose. Now, they are still. He rarely looks at me directly, his gaze fixed somewhere on the wall behind my head, as if watching a distant horizon. His wife, Lien, who brought him here, says he was once a man of easy laughter, a man who smelled of salt and sun. The man in my office is quiet, his presence heavy with a silence that feels older than his years.

For over four decades, the sea was his life. He and his boat, the *Sao Mai*, were constants in the small coastal community. He knew the shifting moods of the water better than he knew the faces of his neighbors. It was a language he understood, a rhythm he moved to. The sea had given him everything: a livelihood, a sense of pride, and a legacy to pass on to his only son, Minh. Minh had grown up on the deck of the *Sao Mai*, learning the trade at his father's side. He had the same steady hands, the same quiet respect for the ocean's power.

The change came eight months ago, on a Tuesday that had started like any other. The sky was a hazy gray, the forecast clear enough. He and Minh were out near the canyons, pulling in a good haul. Mr. Tran remembers the specific shade of green on the water, the way the diesel engine hummed its familiar song. He remembers turning to tell Minh to secure a loose line when the rogue wave hit. It wasn't part of a storm, just a freak swell that rose up from the placid surface, a wall of water that seemed to come from nowhere. It crashed over the stern, a violent, chaotic force. One moment, Minh was there, bracing himself by the winch. The next, he was gone.

Mr. Tran's narrative of that day comes in fractured pieces, delivered in a low, halting monotone. He speaks of the roar of the water, the frantic, useless scan of the churning surface, the name he screamed until his throat was raw. He circled the *Sao Mai* for hours, his eyes burning from the wind and the unshed tears, long after the Coast Guard had arrived and told him there was no hope.

He sold the *Sao Mai* the following week. He couldn't bear to look at it, let alone set foot on its deck. Now, his days are rigidly structured to avoid any reminder of his former life. He wakes before dawn, a habit ingrained from years of fishing, but instead of heading to the docks, he sits in the kitchen, staring into a cold cup of tea. His wife says he won't walk near the harbor and flinches if a car backfires, the sharp sound too much like the crack of a winch cable snapping. He has lost weight, the robust frame that once pulled heavy nets now seeming hollowed out.

Sleep offers no escape. Lien describes his thrashing, his muffled shouts in Vietnamese-short, sharp commands to 'hold on.' He often wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding, the image of his son's face, wide-eyed and shocked, seared behind his eyelids. During the day, he is a ghost in his own home. He feels a profound, gnawing guilt that he cannot articulate but that is visible in the slump of his shoulders. He was the captain. He was the father. He was responsible. The joy he once took in his grandchildren now feels distant, a language he no longer speaks. He watches them play, his face a mask of weary sorrow, convinced he is a failure who couldn't protect his own son from the very force that had sustained their family for generations. His hands, once his greatest tools, now just lie in his lap, a constant, idle reminder of all that he has lost.
